00:00 Case number 25-5133. Vertex Pharmaceuticals Incorporated Appellant v. United States Department of Health and Human Services et al. Mr. Hallward-Drehmeier for the appellant. Mr. Winnick for the appellees.

00:18 Good morning.

00:20 Good morning. May it please the Court. Doug Hallward-Drehmeier on behalf of Appellant Vertex. I'd like to reserve two minutes of my time for rebuttal.

00:29 The District Court recognized that the purpose of the AKS is to prevent the providing or purchasing of health care services that are medically inappropriate in exchange for financial rewards.

00:44 The government doesn't disagree with that. It actually quoted the same language in its brief. And in another case, in the First Circuit, the same government counsel was even more candid.

00:53 It said that the point of the AKS is that financial conflicts in and of themselves corrupt medical decision making.

01:04 If this Court agrees with those characterizations of the AKS, then it has to set aside the OIG's advisory opinion here.

01:12 Because OIG rejected the notion that the AKS requires anything inappropriate or corrupting, mere influence over medical decision making is a crime under the analysis OIG applied.

01:29 OIG's construction cannot be squared with the text of the AKS. And that's where I want to start.

01:36 The AKS starts in paragraph B-1 by criminalizing the solicitation or acceptance of remuneration, including any kickback, bribe, or rebate, in return for providing, purchasing, or referring medically, federally reimbursed health care.

02:02 Paragraph B-2, which is the provision of issue here, is the flip side of the same coin.

02:10 Congress criminalized offering or paying, quote, remuneration, including any kickback, bribe, or rebate, to induce such a referral or purchase.

02:20 In other words, soliciting an unlawful referral or purchase in violation of B-1. B-2 and B-1 operate as a complete whole.

02:31 And Congress's use of the trio of examples, kickback, bribe, or rebate, in both provisions, and its phrase remuneration to induce, which is the obverse of in return for in B-1, confirmed that AKS's two prohibitions operate together to prohibit both sides of a corrupt transaction that distorts medical decision making from the medical merits.

02:56 Can I ask a hypothetical that's been on my mind?

03:00 So if Vertex just, let's assume that the cost of the gene therapy is a million dollars, and let's assume that the cost of fertility treatment is $70,000.

03:10 If Vertex had just reduced the cost of the gene therapy by $70,000, it means that the government, through Medicare, Medicare, Medicare, Medicaid, would pay $70,000 less.

03:26 So that would be a win for the government.

03:30 It wouldn't necessarily be a win for the patient, though, because the government doesn't cover fertility treatments, so that would be $70,000 out of pocket for the patient.
